claims.text: Cypraea tigris schilderiana C. N. Cate, 1961 is currently recognized as an accepted subspecies of Cypraea tigris Linnaeus, 1758, per the WoRMS/MolluscaBase taxonomic database.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS REST API record for AphiaID 574019 returns status:"accepted", rank:"Subspecies", and parentNameUsageID:216843, which itself resolves to the accepted species Cypraea tigris. Both records were retrieved directly from the machine-readable AphiaRecordByAphiaID endpoint, not inferred from a search snippet.

claims.text: The Hawaiian tiger cowrie subspecies was first formally described by C. N. Cate in 1961, in a short paper in The Veliger naming it as a new Hawaiian subspecies of Cypraea tigris.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS's AphiaSourcesByAphiaID list for 574019 cites Cate (1961), Veliger 3(4):107-108, pl.9, with use:"original description" — this is the formal taxonomic act that established the subspecies.

claims.text: The subspecies status of Cypraea tigris schilderiana has been reaffirmed in more recent peer-reviewed taxonomic literature, separate from the original 1961 description.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS cites Meyer & Tweedt (2017), Acta Conchyliorum 16:59-68, with use:"status source" for AphiaID 574019. The full paper text was not independently retrieved, so the specific reasoning for reaffirmation is not verified beyond the WoRMS citation itself — confidence set to moderate rather than high.

claims.text: The type locality of Cypraea tigris schilderiana is Hawaii, and its confirmed distribution centers on the Hawaiian Islands, distinguishing it geographically from the broader Indo-Pacific range of the parent species Cypraea tigris.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS AphiaDistributionsByAphiaID/574019 lists two valid locality records: "Hawaiian Islands" (North Pacific Ocean) and "Hawaii" with typeStatus:"holotype", both with qualityStatus:"checked". The parent species Cypraea tigris is a separate, far more widely distributed Indo-Pacific taxon.

claims.text: In cowries generally, the mantle (a soft extension of the animal's body) can spread out and cover the entire outer shell surface while the animal is active, and this ongoing coverage and maintenance by the mantle is how the shell surface is kept smooth and glossy during life.
claims.evidenceNote: reefs-tiger-cowrie states the mantle "will completely cover its shell unless it feels threatened," at the species (Cypraea tigris) level. marinelifephotography-cowries corroborates the family-level mantle/shell relationship. Neither source is a peer-reviewed biomineralization paper, so confidence is moderate and scope is kept at family/species rather than claimed for the subspecies specifically. Narrowed to drop an earlier unconditional "gloss fades once dead" statement: dead/beachworn shells can remain glossy for a long time, and dulling depends on abrasion, erosion, and environmental exposure rather than death alone, so that claim is not supported as an unconditional rule by these sources.

claims.text: Juvenile cowries look very different from adults: they begin as thin, open, visibly coiled shells resembling small olive shells, and only take on the smooth, rounded, egg-like adult cowrie shape as the animal matures and the outer lip thickens inward.
claims.evidenceNote: Direct quote basis: "Juveniles look nothing like adults, resembling paper-thin olive shells. Coiling as they grow until maturity, when the outer lip turns inward, forms teeth, and the shell thickens..." This is a family-level (Cypraeidae) description from a single specialist field-naturalist source, not a peer-reviewed developmental study, hence moderate confidence.

claims.text: The narrow, tooth-lined aperture (opening) on the underside of a mature cowrie shell forms as part of the maturation process, when the outer lip curls inward and thickens; this toothed margin is a maturity feature, not present on the early juvenile shell.
claims.evidenceNote: marinelifephotography-cowries: outer lip "turns inward, forms teeth, and the shell thickens." reefs-tiger-cowrie independently notes the Cypraea tigris aperture is "lined with 'threatening' tooth-like structures." Combined these support the claim at family/species level; subspecies-specific documentation was not found.

claims.text: In cowries, a shell's overall length is understood to become fixed once the animal reaches maturity and the outer lip thickens; further growth after that point is mainly in shell width and thickness rather than additional length, and the point at which an individual juvenile stops coiling (and thus its final length) varies between individuals.
claims.evidenceNote: Direct quote basis: "The length of an adult cowry is finalized at this point, and additional growth is limited to width and thickness... young cowries stop coiling at random lengths, resulting in mature shells of varying size." This is a single specialist source's general description for the family, not a controlled study, hence moderate confidence.

claims.text: This demo does not have a validated length-to-age model. Size alone does not supply a defensible exact age.
claims.evidenceNote: Methodological statement about this project's scope, not a biological finding: no peer-reviewed, subspecies-specific length-at-age calibration for Cypraea tigris schilderiana was located during this research (searches covering WoRMS source lists, the original 1961 description citation, and specialist cowrie references returned none). Independently, marinelifephotography-cowries notes that individual cowries stop coiling (and thus reach final length) at varying points, which is consistent with size not being a reliable age proxy even in general cowrie biology.

claims.text: Published field reference figures for Cypraea tigris schilderiana describe an average adult length around 100 mm (about 4 in), a maximum of about 153 mm (about 6 in), and note that specimens exceeding roughly 125 mm (about 5 in) are considered rare.
claims.evidenceNote: Direct quote basis: "attains at least 6 inches, 153 mm, while the average is 4 inches, 100 mm. Specimens exceeding 5 inches, 125 mm, are rare and highly desirable." This is a single specialist field-naturalist source rather than a peer-reviewed population survey, so treat these figures as a commonly cited reference range rather than a verified statistical distribution. These figures are close to, but not identical to, informally reported ranges of 90-153 mm / >120 mm rare; only the figures directly verified here (100 mm average, 153 mm maximum, >125 mm rare) are included.

claims.text: Cypraea tigris is commonly found on or near coral reef structures, including resting in crevices and among coral heads, and individuals are sometimes found clustered together.
claims.evidenceNote: marinelifephotography-schilderiana: "Locally common next to coral heads or within crevices in clear water at any depth. Shells tend to occur in clusters." reefs-tiger-cowrie: found "under rocks or resting on soft corals during the day." Both are specialist (non-peer-reviewed) field/aquarium sources; described at the species level since neither source specifically isolates Hawaiian-subspecies habitat data from the wider species.

claims.text: Cypraea tigris individuals are typically more active and forage for food at night, spending daylight hours hidden in crevices or under rocks/corals with the mantle retracted.
claims.evidenceNote: marinelifephotography-schilderiana: "the mantle is usually retracted during the day." reefs-tiger-cowrie: found resting during the day, "foraging for food mostly at night." Two independent specialist sources agree on this pattern at the species level; no subspecies-specific behavioral study was located.

claims.text: Cypraea tigris is omnivorous/opportunistic: juveniles are reported to graze on algae, while adults are reported to feed on sponges, soft corals, and anemones, as well as scavenging leftover meaty material.
claims.evidenceNote: Based on a single aquarium-hobbyist specialist source (reefs-tiger-cowrie) describing captive feeding behavior/diet; this is useful husbandry-based observation but not a peer-reviewed dietary study of wild populations, so confidence is limited and the claim is kept at species level.

claims.text: The cited historical account of cowrie shells used as currency and trade valuables across Africa, South Asia, and parts of the Pacific/Indo-Pacific region documents this monetary role specifically for small cowries — principally the money cowrie (historically placed in Cypraea, now Monetaria moneta) and the ring cowrie (Monetaria annulus) — and does not establish or describe that same monetary role for the much larger tiger cowrie Cypraea tigris or its Hawaiian subspecies.
claims.evidenceNote: conchsoc-shell-money explicitly names "the Money Cowrie (C. moneta) and Ring Cowrie (C. annulus)" as the species that "have circulated as currency in more places in the world than any coin," tracing use from China (1200-800 BC) and India to Africa from roughly the 10th century onward. This single source never attributes currency use to Cypraea tigris or any tiger-cowrie subspecies, so the claim is scoped to what this particular account does and does not document (other-cowries), rather than asserting a universal negative that the tiger cowrie was never used as currency anywhere in history — that broader negative was not independently researched.

claims.text: This manifest and the associated demo do not assign a rarity score, monetary valuation, or population-prevalence estimate to any given shell size; none of the sources consulted provide a verified basis for such figures for this subspecies.
claims.evidenceNote: Methodological statement: no reliable, population-level rarity/valuation data specific to Cypraea tigris schilderiana was found during this research. The only quantitative size notes located (see size-reference-schilderiana) describe a single field reference's reported range and qualitative rarity above ~125 mm, which is not a statistical prevalence study and is not treated as one here.

claims.text: A real-world look-alike for tiger cowries is the panther/leopard cowrie, Cypraea pantherina — a distinct, currently accepted species in the same genus, not a Cypraea tigris subspecies.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS AphiaRecordsByName confirms Cypraea pantherina (AphiaID 216812) as an accepted species in genus Cypraea, with its own parentNameUsageID (205978, the genus), separate from Cypraea tigris (216843) and Cypraea tigris schilderiana (574019). This narrow taxonomic-acceptance statement is backed only by the WoRMS taxonomic database, hence high confidence.

claims.text: Cypraea pantherina is reported to have a similarly large, heavy, glossy, densely dark-spotted shell and a white, finely tooth-lined aperture to Cypraea tigris, making the two look confusable at a glance despite being different species.
claims.evidenceNote: redseacreatures-pantherina describes it as 'a heavy glossy oval, pale under a dense pattern of dark brown spots... The base is white, and the narrow opening is lined with fine teeth along its whole length' — a shell plan close enough to Cypraea tigris to require careful comparison rather than a glance. This morphological/confusability description rests on a single specialist field-identification source rather than a peer-reviewed comparative study, so confidence is moderate, distinct from the high-confidence taxonomic-acceptance fact in lookalike-pantherina-identity.

claims.text: A reported identification cue for Cypraea pantherina is a blurred reddish line running down the middle of the shell's back; this line is not a color marking but the seam where the two halves of the live animal's mantle meet as they fold up and over the shell.
claims.evidenceNote: Direct quote basis: "A blurred reddish line runs down the middle of the back, which is not a marking but a seam: it is where the two halves of the mantle meet when they fold up over the shell from below." Single specialist (non-peer-reviewed) field source, so this is reported as a described cue rather than a verified universal diagnostic across all individuals.

claims.text: Reported size envelopes differ across these look-alike forms: the nominal Cypraea tigris is described as reaching under about 127 mm (5 in), the Hawaiian Cypraea tigris schilderiana as reaching about 100 mm on average and up to about 153 mm, and Cypraea pantherina as usually about 60 mm and occasionally up to about 120 mm — overlapping ranges that make size alone an imperfect single cue.
claims.evidenceNote: marinelifephotography-tigris-nominal: nominal form 'Attains less than 5 inches.' marinelifephotography-schilderiana: schilderiana 'attains at least 6 inches, 153 mm, while the average is 4 inches, 100 mm.' redseacreatures-pantherina: pantherina 'usually 6 cm (2.4 in) and occasionally reaching 12 cm (4.7 in).' All three figures come from single specialist field sources rather than population surveys, and their ranges overlap (e.g. a 120 mm shell could plausibly be a large pantherina or a mid-sized schilderiana), so this is reported as an approximate, imperfect cue rather than a strict dividing line.

claims.text: Geographic range is a useful but not fully exclusive identification cue between these look-alikes: WoRMS distribution records place Cypraea pantherina specifically in the Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, Somali, and Eritrean waters, while Cypraea tigris schilderiana's only checked distribution records are in Hawaii — but WoRMS also carries a separate, checked Red Sea distribution record for the nominal species Cypraea tigris itself, so locality alone does not cleanly separate every tiger-cowrie-like shell.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS AphiaDistributionsByAphiaID/216812 (pantherina) lists Red Sea (x2), Somali EEZ, and Eritrean EEZ, all recordStatus:"valid". WoRMS AphiaDistributionsByAphiaID/216843 (nominal Cypraea tigris) also lists a Red Sea record with qualityStatus:"checked" (the schilderiana-specific distribution list only contains Hawaii records). redseacreatures-pantherina separately states 'Where its close relative the Tiger Cowry turns up in the same waters, the two do not share ground,' suggesting local microhabitat/niche separation even where broad ranges nominally overlap; this nuance is reported rather than resolved, since no source consulted reconciles the two records directly.

claims.text: A mollusc shell is built by the mantle, a tissue layer lining the inside of the shell: cells in the mantle secrete the proteins (and in some layers chitin) that form an organic scaffold, together with calcium carbonate that mineralizes within that scaffold, and the animal grows its shell incrementally over its lifetime rather than shedding and replacing it.
claims.evidenceNote: Direct quote basis, smithsonian-seashell-formation (quoting Chris Meyer, Smithsonian NMNH research zoologist and curator of mollusks): "It all starts in the mantle, the thin layer of flesh connecting a mollusk to its shell. Cells in the mantle secrete all the proteins, chitin, and minerals necessary to create the shell. Mollusks never shed their shells, so the creatures must increase their shell's size as they grow." whoi-seashell-formation independently corroborates: "Calcium carbonate...binds to the protein... the mantle secretes different proteins for different layers." Both are directly fetched, museum/research-institution sources describing molluscs generally (not cowrie- or subspecies-specific), hence scope "mollusks".

claims.text: Experiments on California mussels (Mytilus californianus) demonstrate repair of shell damage in a living mollusc; microscopy found new shell growth around fractures in some experimentally stressed animals. This is evidence from a bivalve, not a cowrie repair timetable or a diagnosis of this demo's hypothetical mark.
claims.evidenceNote: Crane, Diaz Reyes and Denny (2021), abstract and introduction, directly document mechanical recovery after experimental fatigue and shell deposition around fractures in a subset of Mytilus californianus. Repair mechanisms were only partially explained. No experimental repair times, percentages, or species-specific responses are transferred to cowries, and no observed injury is claimed for the procedural illustration.

claims.text: A mollusc shell is protective armor, not simply an empty container: it helps the living animal withstand physical threats, and accumulated damage can affect its mechanical strength.
claims.evidenceNote: The directly read abstract and introduction of Crane, Diaz Reyes and Denny (2021) frame mollusc shells as protective armor and experimentally show weakening after fatigue in California mussels. This general functional explanation does not assert a measured defensive benefit for specific cowrie teeth, colors, or shell shapes.

claims.text: Aragonitic gastropod shells, including the crossed-lamellar type common in many sea snails, are described in the biomaterials literature as consisting mostly of aragonite (a calcium carbonate mineral) with only a small organic fraction, cited at roughly 1 to 5 percent by weight.
claims.evidenceNote: Direct quote basis: "Both nacre and crossed lamellar based shells primarily consist of aragonitic calcium carbonate and a small fraction of organic (polysaccharide and proteinaceous) material (~1-5% (Addadi et al., 2006))." This is a background statement in a materials-science paper whose own experiments are on the queen conch (Strombus gigas), citing an earlier literature figure (Addadi et al. 2006) rather than a new measurement of the paper's own; no Cypraea-specific percentage was found. Schema scope is recorded as "mollusks" (the closest available scope value), but the underlying evidence is specifically about gastropods (sea snails), not molluscs generally (e.g., not verified for bivalves or cephalopods), and the figure is presented as a commonly cited range rather than a universal constant.

claims.text: In gastropod shells, a small organic matrix of proteins and polysaccharides is not just filler: research describes it as providing a pathway that controls the growth and arrangement of the calcium carbonate mineral crystals, which is part of why biological shell is much tougher than non-living mineral of the same chemical type.
claims.evidenceNote: Direct quote basis: "These organics afforded a pathway to control the growth and arrangement of the CaCO3 mineral components... and thus enabled gastropods to evolve numerous shell microstructures with increasing toughness versus its geologic counterpart." General gastropod-class statement from a paper about Strombus gigas; not verified specifically for Cypraeidae. Scope is recorded as "mollusks" (the closest available schema value), but the evidence is gastropod-specific, not verified across molluscs generally.

claims.text: A gastropod does not grow a new shell from scratch: its existing shell is enlarged by its mantle, which adds new material at the shell's growing margin (the edge nearest the body opening), so the shell gets bigger by extension at that edge rather than by swelling all over.
claims.evidenceNote: whoi-seashell-formation: "As the animal grows, its shell must grow along with it. This happens along the outer edges. A snail adds to its shell around the opening, where it pokes its head out." charleston-biol337-mollusca independently corroborates: "a gastropod literally grows out of the aperture of its shell, adding new material to the edge of the shell." The specific technical term "extrapallial space" was not found in any source fetched directly during this research, so it is not used in this claim; the underlying mechanism (mantle-driven growth at the shell margin) is instead stated in the plain language the sources themselves use. This complements, rather than duplicates, material-shell-secretion, which covers the chemical/cellular secretion mechanism rather than the growth location. Scope is recorded as "mollusks" (the closest available schema value); both direct sources describe gastropods specifically, not molluscs generally.

claims.text: The outermost layer of a typical mollusc/gastropod shell is mostly organic (protein, sometimes described as the protein conchiolin) rather than mineral, and it is produced by the mantle at the shell's growing edge as the animal enlarges its shell; in gastropods this organic layer is called the periostracum.
claims.evidenceNote: Direct quote basis, charleston-biol337-mollusca: "the thin brown outer periostracum composed of the protein conchiolin" (illustrated on a prepared clam-shell cross-section slide, but stated to reflect general mollusc shell properties). whoi-seashell-formation independently corroborates that "the outermost layer is mostly protein" and that shell growth happens at the outer edge. Neither source explicitly states that the periostracum is laid down chronologically before the mineral layers beneath it at that edge, so this claim is limited to layer identity/composition and growth location rather than deposition sequence; no cowrie-specific periostracum description was found. Scope is recorded as "mollusks" (the closest available schema value); the charleston-biol337-mollusca example is illustrated on a clam shell but stated to reflect general mollusc shell properties, while "periostracum" as a named layer is specifically a gastropod-shell term.

claims.text: In cowries, including Cypraea tigris, the mantle that spreads over the shell deposits new outer shell material (described by one family-level source as "a coat of enamel") that keeps the surface glossy, and a dorsal furrow/line is a recognized shell feature on the back of cowries where this mantle coverage is centered.
claims.evidenceNote: txmarspecies-cypraeidae: "the snail covers the shell with its mantle which continually deposits a coat of enamel and protects the shell from wear and tear" (family-level, Cypraeidae). fao-gastropods-leal glossary: "Furrow - groove in longitudinal direction found on the dorsal region of, among other shells, cowries..." (names cowries specifically for this dorsal feature). reefs-tiger-cowrie adds species-level (Cypraea tigris) detail that the extended mantle appears "like a fingerprint of black and gray, with many short papillae over the surface." Combined, these support mantle-driven gloss and a dorsal line/furrow feature for cowries generally, with one species-specific (C. tigris) mantle-pattern detail; this is additional corroboration alongside the existing mantle-coating-and-polish claim, not a replacement for it.

claims.text: An independent family-level source corroborates that juvenile cowries have a wider aperture and a thin outer lip, that the outer lip thickens and curves inward at maturity, and that cowries can mature (stop lengthening) at different sizes depending on factors such as temperature and food, producing some undersized "dwarf" adult shells.
claims.evidenceNote: Direct quote basis: "Juvenile cowries are distinctly different from adults. Their aperture is wider and the outer lip is thin. When the cowrie becomes an adult, its outer lip thickens and curves inward. Cowries can mature at different sizes depending on factors such as temperature and food sources. Those that mature at smaller sizes are called dwarf shells." This independently corroborates (from a different, government/university-hosted source) the existing juvenile-to-adult-shape-change, aperture-teeth-at-maturity, and length-finalized-at-maturity claims, which were previously sourced only to marinelifephotography.com; family scope, not subspecies-specific.

claims.text: Cowries such as Cypraea tigris have a head-foot like other snails of their kind, with a pair of cephalic tentacles and eyes on the head and a muscular foot for crawling; the family's shell has a narrow siphonate aperture associated with an anterior siphon, and in Cypraea tigris specifically the two extended mantle lobes covering the shell are patterned with short papillae.
claims.evidenceNote: ucmp-gastropoda-morphology and charleston-biol337-mollusca are general, class-level (Gastropoda) descriptions of the head (cephalic tentacles, eyes) and an anteriorly-extended mantle-edge siphon, not cowrie-specific; they are combined here with family-specific evidence. nutzel-et-al-2025-cypraeoid-origin directly states, for Cypraeidae, a "narrow, slit-like siphonate aperture with anterior and posterior canals." reefs-tiger-cowrie directly describes the Cypraea tigris mantle as appearing "like a fingerprint of black and gray, with many short papillae over the surface." The cephalic-tentacle/eye detail is therefore a generalization from typical gastropod anatomy applied to cowries, not independently verified for Cypraeidae in the sources read, and is flagged as such; the siphonate aperture and mantle papillae are directly cowrie/species-sourced.

claims.text: In gastropods generally, the mantle cavity houses the ctenidium (gill) and osphradium (a chemosensory organ), while the visceral mass inside the shell's whorls contains the gonad, digestive gland, heart, kidney, and part of the digestive tract; Cypraeidae specifically have a taenioglossate radula (a ribbon of small rasping teeth), and adult cowries, including Cypraea tigris, lack an operculum (the trapdoor-like plate many other snails use to seal the shell opening).
claims.evidenceNote: fao-gastropods-leal: "the mantle cavity...[is] where the ctenidium (or ctenidia), osphradium, anus, nephridiopore, and external genitalia are located. The visceral mass...is the location of the gonads, digestive gland, heart, kidney, and part of the alimentary system." charleston-biol337-mollusca independently corroborates the mantle cavity/ctenidia/visceral-mass organization at class level. nutzel-et-al-2025-cypraeoid-origin states Cypraeidae "have a taenioglossate radula," a family-specific, peer-reviewed detail. reefs-tiger-cowrie (species, Cypraea tigris: "does not have an operculum") and txmarspecies-cypraeidae (family, Cypraeidae: "The aperture has no operculum") independently corroborate operculum absence at two taxonomic levels. The general organ list is class-level (gastropods specifically, not molluscs generally; scope is recorded as "mollusks" as the closest available schema value), while the radula and operculum details are specifically cowrie-sourced, as noted.

claims.text: An adult cowrie shell is convolute: its last whorl grows over and encloses all of the earlier whorls, hiding the juvenile spiral shape inside the smooth adult shell. No directly verified source describes internal resorption of the earlier whorls in cowries, so that process is not claimed here.
claims.evidenceNote: Direct quote basis: "Cowries are conspicuous in having a convolute shell, with the last whorl enclosing all previous whorls and forming a narrowly elongate, slit-like aperture..." This is a peer-reviewed, family-level (Cypraeidae) statement. Internal septum/wall resorption during cowrie growth was searched for specifically but not found in any source read directly during this research, so, per instructions, no resorption claim is made; this is stated as an explicit omission rather than a negative scientific finding.

claims.text: This demo's procedural illustration is a simplified, single-subspecies growth visualization and is not sufficient on its own to distinguish Cypraea tigris schilderiana from similar-looking cowries such as Cypraea pantherina or the nominal Cypraea tigris; real-world identification depends on combined evidence such as locality, precise spot pattern, and shell proportions, ideally checked against a reference collection or specialist.
claims.evidenceNote: Methodological statement about this project's scope: the research above shows that size, dorsal pattern, and even broad geographic range each have exceptions or overlaps (see lookalike-size-envelope-differs and lookalike-range-not-fully-exclusive), so no single cue — and certainly not a procedural illustration built around one reference subspecies — is adequate for confident species/subspecies discrimination.

claims.text: Cypraea tigris Linnaeus, 1758 is the currently accepted name for the tiger cowrie in the family Cypraeidae, per the World Register of Marine Species.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS AphiaRecord (AphiaID 216843) lists the name as accepted, not a synonym, with authority Linnaeus, 1758; checked directly on the AphiaRecord page.

claims.text: Adult Cypraea tigris shells are reported to reach up to about 150 mm (6 in), though one specialist field guide describes the widespread (non-Hawaiian) form as topping out under 127 mm (5 in).
claims.evidenceNote: Wikipedia's species account states the shell 'measures up to 15 cm (6in)'; marinelifephotography.com's field page instead gives 'less than 5 inches' for the species generally and 'nearly 6 inches' specifically for the separately-covered Hawaiian subspecies. The two reported maxima do not fully agree, so this is reported as a range of figures rather than one confirmed number.

claims.text: The adult dorsal shell surface is white, pale bluish-white, or buff, densely covered with dark brown to blackish rounded spots, with a glossy, polished-looking surface; a faint red line sometimes runs along the dorsal midline.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from the Wikipedia species account's description section; a tertiary source, but consistent with the spotted pattern implied by the common name 'tiger cowrie' and with cowrie shell gloss described elsewhere for the family.

claims.text: Cypraea tigris is described as common under dead coral in shallow water across the Indo-West Pacific.
claims.evidenceNote: Short field-guide habitat note read directly from marinelifephotography.com's Cypraea tigris page; a single specialist/diver-naturalist source, not a population survey.

claims.text: In a 2023 laboratory study, female Cypraea tigris brooded (sat over) their egg masses for 7 to 17 days, remaining with the capsules until the larvae hatched; disturbed brooders sometimes abandoned or consumed their own egg mass.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from the 'Brooding and spawning' discussion section of Tay et al. 2023 (PMC10090884), a peer-reviewed captive-breeding study of this exact species.

claims.text: Lab-reared Cypraea tigris veliger larvae survived free-swimming for up to 37 days without completing metamorphosis or settling; the natural length of the planktonic larval stage and any settlement cue remain undetermined.
claims.evidenceNote: Directly confirmed from the same 2023 peer-reviewed study: the authors report their longest-surviving C. tigris larvae 'lasted up to just 37 days' with 'stagnated development,' unlike the related Mauritia arabica reared in the same experiment, which did metamorphose.

claims.text: Monetaria moneta (Linnaeus, 1758) is the currently accepted name for the money cowrie; the older, still widely used name Cypraea moneta is now treated as a synonym under the genus Monetaria.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS AphiaRecord (AphiaID 216874) checked directly; genus placement differs from the older 'Cypraea moneta.'

claims.text: Reported adult size for Monetaria moneta ranges from about 30 mm per one general reference up to 45 mm (1.8 in) in a Hawaii-based field account; a single consistent typical size is not established.
claims.evidenceNote: marinelifephotography.com states 'Attains 1.8 inches, 45mm'; Wikipedia's species account instead describes it as 'up to 3cm (1.2in).' Both were read directly; the figures disagree, so no single number is asserted as definitive.

claims.text: The small, flattened shell is pale (white to dirty beige), with a dorsum that can look semi-transparent, often greenish-grey with yellowish margins and sometimes darker transverse stripes and a faint yellow ring; the underside is white with pronounced denticles. The living animal's mantle shows a vivid mottled or zebra-like black-and-white pattern.
claims.evidenceNote: Shell description read directly from Wikipedia's 'Description and characteristics' section; mantle description cross-checked against marinelifephotography.com's field note calling it an 'attractive zebra-striped' mantle pattern.

claims.text: Monetaria moneta grazes on algae-covered rocks in broad daylight on shallow reefs and intertidal rocky areas/tide pools, unlike some nocturnal cowrie species; a Hawaii-focused field account describes it as locally uncommon around Hawaii/Maui but abundant elsewhere across its Indo-Pacific range.
claims.evidenceNote: Daytime algae-grazing behaviour read directly from marinelifephotography.com; intertidal/tide-pool habitat corroborated by Wikipedia's ecology section, which itself cites Poutiers (1998, FAO guide) that I was not able to access directly.

claims.text: Money cowrie shells were historically used as currency (shell money) across many Pacific and Indian Ocean societies, a use that persisted into the 1800s before being displaced by coinage.
claims.evidenceNote: Both sources state this directly and consistently: marinelifephotography.com ('Used as currency in many countries until the 1800's') and Wikipedia ('historically widely used...as shell money before coinage was in common usage').

claims.text: Conus textile Linnaeus, 1758 is the currently accepted name for the textile cone in the family Conidae.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS AphiaRecord (AphiaID 215529) checked directly; listed as accepted, not a synonym.

claims.text: Conus textile has a shell with a concave spire that is white with golden blotches and dark brown tent-like markings; the living animal is white mottled with tan, and its siphon is banded black and red. Reported maximum size is about 150 mm (6 in).
claims.evidenceNote: Description and size figure read directly from marinelifephotography.com's Conus textile page; a single Hawaii-based specialist field account, not a formal taxonomic redescription.

claims.text: Conus textile is classified among the molluscivorous (mollusc-eating) cone snails; a review of cone snail venom biology reports it stores about 75 radular harpoon-teeth in its venom apparatus (29 in the short arm, 46 in the long arm of the radular sac), more than the vermivorous and piscivorous species tabulated in the same review.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from Table 1 and its surrounding text in Dutertre & Lewis (2013); the larger radular-tooth stock is linked in the text to molluscivorous species' capacity for repeated stinging of armoured prey.

claims.text: Across the genus Conus, eggs are laid roughly once a year in capsules attached to the substrate; one cited study (on two other cone species, not C. textile) found egg masses of up to 25 capsules with up to 1,000 eggs each, so roughly 25,000 eggs per mass.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from the 'Reproductive Biology' section of Dutertre & Lewis (2013); the specific egg-count figures are attributed in the text to Zehra & Perveen (1991), a paper on Conus biliosus and C. coronatus, not C. textile, so this is reported at family/genus level rather than as a confirmed C. textile figure.

claims.text: The free-swimming (pelagic) veliger stage of Conus species is reported to last between about 1 and 50 days before settlement, based on a study of a different cone species (C. pennaceus); C. textile larvae have, separately, been reared through this planktonic stage in captivity under controlled feeding and water-flow conditions.
claims.evidenceNote: The 1-50 day pelagic-duration figure is attributed in the review to Perron (1983), a study of Conus pennaceus, so it is reported at genus/family level. The captive-rearing note is specific to C. textile and attributed to Perron (1980), 'Laboratory culture of the larvae of Conus textile,' cited directly in the same review; I could not independently access Perron (1980)'s full text, so no specific day-count is asserted for C. textile itself.

claims.text: A standard reference on living Conidae estimates cone snail lifespan at roughly 10 to 20 years in the wild and in captivity, based on shell growth rate and growth marks; this figure spans the genus and is not confirmed specifically for C. textile.
claims.evidenceNote: Figure attributed to Rockel, Korn & Kohn (1995), Manual of the Living Conidae, as cited and read directly in Dutertre & Lewis (2013).

claims.text: Of roughly 700 Conus species, only Conus geographus has been confirmed responsible for multiple human fatalities; a 2018 peer-reviewed review found that older reports attributing human deaths specifically to C. textile have not been adequately verified, and molluscivorous cone species as a group are generally considered far less dangerous to humans than fish-hunting species.
claims.evidenceNote: Directly read from Kohn (2018), 'Conus Envenomation of Humans: In Fact and Fiction,' Toxins (PMC6356772), a peer-reviewed review of all documented human Conus stings 1670-2017; corroborated by Dutertre & Lewis (2013), which separately states 'only Conus geographus has been confirmed as responsible for several human deaths.'

claims.text: A photographed Conus textile shell from Hawaii shows a hole captioned by the photographer as an 'octopus bite,' illustrating one way a cone snail shell can be damaged during or after a predation attempt; this is a single photographed specimen, not a population-level predation study.
claims.evidenceNote: Caption read directly from a photograph on marinelifephotography.com's Conus textile page; treated as anecdotal single-specimen field evidence, not a verified predation study, and not used to diagnose any particular shell or illustration in this project.

claims.text: A mollusc shell can only grow at its growing edge, and in many species new pigment is added only during this growth process at that edge; patterned stripes or markings on a shell therefore record, in space, a patterning process that played out over time at the growing margin.
claims.evidenceNote: Paraphrased directly from the Scholarpedia article 'Gierer-Meinhardt model,' authored by Hans Meinhardt himself (confirmed via page citation metadata), a peer-reviewed encyclopedia entry describing the general activator-inhibitor model for mollusc shell pigmentation. This is a general mollusc-shell-growth principle, not a Conus textile-specific study, so it is scoped at the mollusks level; it is directly relevant to why cone-shell patterns (like C. textile's) look as they do.

claims.text: After a gastropod dies and its soft tissue is gone, the empty shell is commonly recycled by hermit crabs and other organisms as a portable home or substrate; a 2004 review found over 550 invertebrate species from 16 phyla living in association with hermit-crab-occupied gastropod shells worldwide.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from the abstract of Williams & McDermott (2004), Journal of Experimental Marine Biology and Ecology; a general mollusc-shell-reuse pattern, not specific to cowries or cone snails, so scoped at the mollusks level.

claims.text: The queen conch is now named Aliger gigas (Linnaeus, 1758) in the World Register of Marine Species; the older name Strombus gigas is a superseded combination.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS REST records read directly; NOAA's classification also lists genus Aliger, species gigas, family Strombidae.

claims.text: Queen conch grow up to about 12 inches (about 300 mm) long and up to about 5 pounds. Females on average grow faster and larger than males.
claims.evidenceNote: Stated directly by NOAA Fisheries. 12 inches converted to about 300 mm. NOAA gives a maximum, not a typical range.

claims.text: A large, heavy shell with short spines around the spire and a pink interior to the shell lip. The animal has long eye stalks that move independently, a brown, rough operculum, and a tube-like mouth (proboscis).
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from NOAA's appearance section.

claims.text: Queen conch live throughout the Caribbean Sea, the Florida Keys and around Bermuda. Adults favour sandy algal flats, gravel, coral rubble and beach rock; juveniles live mostly in seagrass beds; they are most common in water less than about 30 m (100 ft) deep where unfished.
claims.evidenceNote: Range and habitat read directly from NOAA. 100 feet converted to about 30 m.

claims.text: After internal fertilisation, a female lays an egg mass over 24 to 36 hours containing on average 500,000 to 750,000 eggs, which hatch after about 5 days.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from NOAA's biology section. Incubation is given as about 5 days.

claims.text: The larvae drift in the water for 21 to 30 days, feeding on phytoplankton, before settling to the bottom and changing into the shelled form.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from NOAA's biology section.

claims.text: Queen conch are thought to mature at around 3.5 to 4 years old. Once mature they stop growing in length: the shell lip only grows thicker.
claims.evidenceNote: NOAA says conch are 'believed to reach sexual maturity around 3.5 to 4 years of age' and notes size at maturity varies with environment; hence moderate confidence. The flared, thickening lip is drawn from this.

claims.text: Queen conch are long-lived, generally reaching 25 to 30 years old.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from NOAA's biology section.

claims.text: Queen conch are heavily fished for their meat, and in 2024 NOAA Fisheries listed them as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act. Check local rules before taking any conch shell, and never take a live animal.
claims.evidenceNote: Listing status read directly from NOAA. The advice to check local rules is a responsible-collecting inference, not a statement of any specific law.

claims.text: The chambered nautilus, Nautilus pompilius Linnaeus, 1758, is a cephalopod: a relative of squid and octopus that keeps an external, coiled, chambered shell.
claims.evidenceNote: WoRMS status accepted; NOAA describes nautiluses as cephalopods related to squids and octopuses, set apart by their coiled shells.

claims.text: Its coiled shell ranges from white to orange and even purple, with its own pattern of colour; more than 90 tentacles without suckers protrude from the opening.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from NOAA's appearance section. Adult shell length is not given in this source, so the simulator draws it at an illustrative size and says so.

claims.text: The nautilus lives in the newest, largest chamber. It uses the older chambers and a tube running through them to control its buoyancy, and swims backwards by jet propulsion.
claims.evidenceNote: NOAA describes buoyancy control with the chambers and a tube running the length of the shell, and backwards jet propulsion. NOAA calls the tube a 'hyponome'; anatomical texts usually call the chamber tube the siphuncle and the jet funnel the hyponome, so the simulator says 'tube' rather than naming it.

claims.text: Chambered nautilus live mainly in the western Pacific Ocean and coastal areas of the Indian Ocean, in small, isolated populations limited by depth and temperature.
claims.evidenceNote: Range read directly from NOAA; WoRMS distribution records include Madagascar, Chagos, Ambon and the Central Indo-Pacific. Depth values are not given in these sources.

claims.text: Unlike other cephalopods, nautiluses live 15 to 20 years or more. They grow slowly, mature at around 10 to 15 years, and lay a small number of eggs that take at least a year to hatch.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from NOAA's lifespan and reproduction section. 'At least a year' is used as a minimum incubation of 365 days.

claims.text: Chambered nautilus have several predators, including sharks, bony fish and octopuses.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from NOAA's species overview.

claims.text: Chambered shells can float after the animal dies. Most nautilus species drift only a little, but Nautilus pompilius shells are found far from known living populations.
claims.evidenceNote: From the abstract of Yacobucci (2018), read in full text: drift shells of N. pompilius are found far from living populations, while most nautilid species show limited drift.

claims.text: Nautilus shells are the main reason the animals are fished: they are traded worldwide for souvenirs, jewellery and decor. In 2018 NOAA listed the chambered nautilus as threatened under the US Endangered Species Act. Avoid buying nautilus shells.
claims.evidenceNote: Trade as the primary threat and the 2018 listing are read directly from NOAA. The advice not to buy shells is a conservation inference from that threat.

claims.text: Predators such as moon snails (naticids), murex snails (muricids), octopuses, crabs and birds can leave holes in mollusc shells.
claims.evidenceNote: From the introduction of the systematic review (Kubicka et al., 2017), which lists hole-boring predators and reviews 54 publications on holes made by non-human predators.

claims.text: Rolling in waves and tides wears shells down; experiments show abrasion alone can make holes that look like a predator's.
claims.evidenceNote: Kubicka et al. (2017) summarise shell-rolling experiments by Gorzelak and co-workers (2013) that imitate waves and tides. Read as a secondary account of that experiment.

claims.text: Exceptionally large Nautilus pompilius shells reach about 254 mm across, recorded from Indonesia and northern Australia; most are smaller.
claims.evidenceNote: A record size, cited by Wikipedia to a shell-record registry not read directly. The simulator draws the nautilus at an illustrative size well below this record and labels it as such.

claims.text: Molluscs form an accepted animal phylum, Mollusca, in the global register of marine species; the species names in this simulator follow the same register (WoRMS / MolluscaBase).
claims.evidenceNote: Machine-readable WoRMS record for AphiaID 51 returns status accepted and rank Phylum. Each species in the simulator carries its own AphiaID claim.

claims.text: About 86,600 living mollusc species are recognised, making molluscs the second-largest animal phylum. Gastropods, the snails, account for about 80% of classified mollusc species.
claims.evidenceNote: Figures read directly from the article lead, which cites its counts. Species counts change as new species are described, so these are approximate.

claims.text: A mollusc's soft body is mostly muscle. Its mantle encloses a cavity used for breathing and excretion and secretes the shell, which is made of proteins and chitin reinforced with calcium carbonate. Most molluscs feed with a rasping radula and move on a single muscular foot.
claims.evidenceNote: From the article's description of the features shared by modern molluscs and its 'hypothetical ancestral mollusc'. Individual groups vary: bivalves lack a radula and cephalopods have arms rather than a crawling foot.

claims.text: Nearly all molluscs lay eggs. Depending on the group, these hatch as trochophore larvae, as more complex veliger larvae, or as miniature adults.
claims.evidenceNote: Read directly from the article's overview of molluscan reproduction. Which route a species takes is given by its own sourced claims where known.

claims.text: The sources used for this simulator do not document how this species usually dies, so this ending names no predator.
claims.evidenceNote: A deliberate gap: predators reported only in unverified summaries were left out rather than presented as fact.

claims.text: GBIF holds 4,193 located records of Cypraea tigris: museum specimens and observations, leaving out fossils and automated tag detections. 30 of the 46 seas and islands shown here have at least one record.
claims.evidenceNote: The counts are facts about the database, not about the ocean. More records usually means more divers, collectors and surveys, not more animals; old museum labels can be imprecise; and empty shells can be recorded far from where the animal lived. A region with no records may simply be unsurveyed. Region outlines are simple boxes drawn for this simulator.

claims.text: A parametric model with six numbers (whorl expansion, distance from the axis, spire translation, aperture ratio, aperture tilt and aperture rotation) reproduces the shell forms of snails, limpets, nautiluses, ammonites and bivalves; the paper gives fitted values for real specimens.
claims.evidenceNote: From the paper's abstract and its published equations. The lab's specimen parameters follow Table 1 as transcribed by the open-source mollusc3d port; the full text could not be fetched automatically to cross-check every value, hence moderate confidence. The model describes shape, not colour.

claims.text: A coiled snail shell begins with the larval shell (protoconch), which forms the apex of the spire; the whorls grow larger from there to the last and largest, the body whorl, which ends at the opening (aperture). The coil turns around a central pillar, the columella, and in some shells the aperture is drawn out into a siphonal canal.
claims.evidenceNote: Part names used by the figure's labels. The article states the protoconch forms the apex of the spire, the spire is the part above the body whorl, and the central axis passes through the columella, the central pillar of the shell.

claims.text: A veliger larva swims and gathers food with a ciliated velum that extends beyond its shell, and can pull the velum and foot back into the shell; it loses the velum at metamorphosis into a juvenile.
claims.evidenceNote: Applies to veliger larvae in general. The tiger cowrie's own larva is not documented (see tiger-cowrie-larva-unresolved), so the figure's velum is generic.

claims.text: A nautilus shell is divided into chambers by thin walls called septa, each pierced in the middle by a tube, the siphuncle. As the animal grows it moves forward into a new living chamber and builds a septum behind it. It can close the opening with a leathery hood formed from two folded tentacles, and swims by pushing water out through its funnel (hyponome).
claims.evidenceNote: Nautilus: septa pierced by the siphuncle, the hood from two folded tentacles, jet propulsion with the hyponome. Septum (cephalopod): the body moves forward to a new living chamber, secreting septa behind it.
